extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety professionals, labor representatives, and stakeholders commenting on OSHA's proposed heat injury and illness prevention standard
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply the criteria and recommended elements of OSHA's proposed heat injury and illness prevention standard and related guidance from federal and consensus organizations. Useful for preparing comments, compliance plans, or program design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-component heat injury and illness prevention program
rubrics_metrics.description: A program that incorporates multiple interventions (engineering, administrative/work-practice, PPE, training, acclimatization, medical surveillance, environmental monitoring, emergency response) to reduce risk of HRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA finds multicomponent interventions more effective for quantitative reductions in HRI because individual components contribute to the overall effect; evidence shows 37–96% reductions in HRI claims in civilian studies and 54–95% in military studies. Program elements summarized in Table V-3 and supported by laboratory/experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written heat injury and illness prevention plan (written exposure control plan / heat safety plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers should develop and implement a written program/plan to prevent heat-related injury and illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple sources (state standards, NIOSH, NACOSH, ACGIH, ANSI/ASSP) recommend a written plan; examples of required contents include general controls, job-specific controls, emergency response procedures, and designation of responsible personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training on heat illness recognition and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide training for workers and supervisors on recognizing HRI, prevention measures, and appropriate responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH, FACE investigations, NACOSH, ANSI/ASSP and others recommend training; OSHA's proposed standard includes training as a core control. Training was part of effective programs described in studies (e.g., HSAP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of readily accessible drinking water
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide cool drinking water (and as appropriate sports drinks/electrolyte supplements) and ensure unlimited access during work shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as a main intervention in proposed standard and in effective programs (McCarthy et al., Bodin et al.); ANSI/ASSP and EPA guidance recommend establishing a drinking water program and coolers with ice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest breaks and shaded or cooled break locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide rest breaks of appropriate frequency and duration in shade or cool-down areas, including a lunch break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly recommended by NIOSH, MSHA, EPA, ANSI/ASSP, ACGIH; examples include scheduled short rests (10-15 min) and longer lunch breaks used in interventions (Bodin et al.). OSHA requests comment on appropriate frequencies/durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization procedures and acclimatization planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement acclimatization protocols for new and returning workers and plan for acclimatization in the written program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACGIH, NIOSH, NACOSH, Military guidance (TRADOC, TB MED 507) recommend acclimatization; interventions that differentiated guidance for acclimatized vs unacclimatized recruits showed large reductions in HRI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental heat monitoring (WBGT and other measures) and use of exposure limits/action limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor environmental heat (e.g., WBGT) and apply exposure limits (TLV, AL, PHEL) or triggers to guide work-rest decisions and other controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH/ACGIH WBGT-based TLV/AL, Navy PHEL curves, and Army TRADOC requirements use WBGT to set rest/shade/water requirements and work stoppage criteria. Examples: using WBGT to pause training, issuing heat alerts when thresholds exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering controls to reduce environmental heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement engineering measures such as ventilation, increased air movement, air-conditioning, exhaust fans, radiant heat shields, screening, insulation, and canopies to reduce heat exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH and ANSI/ASSP list ventilation, air-conditioning, radiant barriers, evaporative controls (misting), and process modifications as preferred controls when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/work-practice controls (work-rest scheduling, task rotation, scheduling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt administrative controls such as work-rest regimens, rotating personnel through hot tasks, scheduling heavy tasks at cooler times, pacing tasks, and allowing self-paced work where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSHA, EPA, ANSI/ASSP, and ACGIH recommend these measures; examples in interventions include structured rest breaks (10–15 minutes) and changing job assignments to reduce metabolic load (efficiency interventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and use of appropriate personal protective equipment and personal cooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide heat-protective clothing/PPE and personal/portable cooling devices when engineering/administrative controls are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH recommends cooling clothing/PPE if other controls don't reduce exposures below RAL/REL; ANSI/ASSP and ASTM recommend personal cooling and PPE appropriate to the job and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical monitoring / medical surveillance and medical clearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement medical surveillance, monitoring, or medical screening to identify workers at increased risk for HRI and provide counseling or restrictions as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH, ACGIH, ANSI/ASSP recommend medical clearance and counseling; McCarthy/Perkison studies suggest medical surveillance may be an important component in lowering workforce HRI (study limitations noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace surveillance, risk assessment, and incident review
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct workplace heat-risk assessments, monitor program effectiveness, evaluate temperature/conditions, issue heat alerts, and review incidents to implement corrective actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ASTM and ANSI/ASSP include workplace surveillance and risk assessment as program elements; EPA guidance recommends evaluating weather, workload, PPE, and employee condition when designing controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency response procedures and first aid for heat illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish emergency response protocols, first aid procedures, and ensure prompt medical assistance (including treatment methods such as iced sheets and cold water/ice-water immersion for exertional heat stroke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NACOSH, NIOSH FACE reports, military and marathon treatment studies demonstrate high survival when effective immediate cooling is provided; OSHA highlights studies showing 99.8–100% survival with rapid cooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buddy system and supervisor monitoring of worker symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a buddy system and require supervisors to monitor worker symptoms and check in regularly to detect early signs of HRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended by ANSI/ASSP, NIOSH, and NACOSH as administrative/communication controls; used in State standards and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of sodium/electrolyte supplements as appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sodium/electrolyte supplements in addition to water when appropriate to reduce risk of electrolyte imbalance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANSI/ASSP specifically recommends provision of sodium electrolyte supplements; used in some successful military and civilian programs; consider medical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of responsible program manager or person
rubrics_metrics.description: Designate one person to manage the heat stress program and ensure program elements are implemented and overseen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA guidance explicitly recommends designating a program manager; written plans should identify responsibilities for implementation and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee participation in program planning and implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Involve workers in planning activities and program implementation to improve effectiveness and acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NACOSH and ANSI/ASSP recommend worker participation; inclusion is mentioned as an element in several consensus documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job-specific controls as part of Heat Stress Management Programs (HSMP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop job-specific controls (engineering, administrative, personal cooling, physiological monitoring) tailored to particular tasks and exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACGIH recommends HSMPs include general controls and, as appropriate, job-specific controls (Table 5 referenced). ASTM similarly lists program elements for foundry environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological monitoring and symptom monitoring to assess heat strain
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement physiological monitoring (where appropriate) and systematic symptom monitoring to detect heat strain in workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACGIH and ASTM reference physiological monitoring; OSHA notes symptom monitoring and supervisor observation as recommended practices; examples include monitoring urine, reports of dizziness, fainting, cramps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consensus exposure limits and action limits (TLV/AL/RAL/REL/PHEL) adjusted for work intensity and clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply exposure/action limits (e.g., ACGIH TLV, AL; NIOSH RAL/REL; Navy PHEL) that account for environmental heat, metabolic heat from work intensity, and clothing/PPE to guide controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACGIH's TLV aims to maintain thermal equilibrium for healthy acclimatized employees; action limits consider unacclimatized employees. NIOSH recommends reducing exposure to or below applicable RAL/REL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement cooling technologies and portable cool-down mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide cooling devices (fans, tents, evaporative misting, portable cool-down units) and cooled rest areas where feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANSI/ASSP and NIOSH list portable cooling options; NACOSH recommended proactive misting and portable cool-down mechanisms; Army/Navy guidance includes shade, fans, iced sheets for treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure program is tailored to workplace and worker population
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor program components (controls, acclimatization, monitoring) to the specific workplace conditions, types of workers (e.g., military vs civilian), and tasks performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes differences between military and civilian populations (fitness, activities, special controls) and that plans should be tailored to each workplace. Several studies varied by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide cool locations for breaks and, when feasible, cooled work areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure availability of cooled locations for rest breaks and, where feasible, provide cooling for indoor workspaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ASTM and MSHA recommend cooled rest areas; examples include air-conditioned restrooms, shaded break canopies, and cooled indoor classrooms used in historical military programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and evaluate program effectiveness and adjust measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Track outcomes (e.g., HRI claims, symptoms, productivity) to evaluate intervention effectiveness and modify the program as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA summarizes study outcomes (claim rate reductions, symptom reductions) and notes program modifications (e.g., removal of medical surveillance increased HRI rates). Standards recommend incident review and corrective action.
